paper.title: When Can We Trust the Matching Principle? Robust Deployment Geometry Under Finite-Sample and Model Uncertainty
paper.abstract:
Abstract Match only geometry you can identify; otherwise spread the penalty.
We quantify that decision by the trust ratio τ = ε / γ \tau=\varepsilon/\gamma (estimation uncertainty over spectral separation).
Under the linear–quadratic Matching response, oracle-relative drift between
estimated and oracle projector matching scales as τ 2 \tau^{2} for probes in the
chosen top- r r deployment subspace— O ⁡ ( τ 2 ) O(\tau^{2}) in the Davis–Kahan
separation region τ < 1 / 2 \tau<1/2 , with practical usefulness depending on
constants.
Confidence-Calibrated Matching (CCM) turns τ \tau into a policy—directional
when τ \tau is small, progressively isotropic when not—with thresholds from
calibration, not from the theorem (match sits in the separation region; soft
is mostly heuristic).
Experiments show both regimes, including UCI HAR embeddings where always-match
is worse than abstain on every cell.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Suppose Matching would be optimal if the deployment direction were known. We estimate it, regularise aggressively—and do worse than isotropic. The problem is not whether directional matching is sharp; it is whether the direction is identifiable. Match only geometry you can identify; otherwise spread the penalty. That is the whole decision. Finite samples scramble subspaces when the eigengap is small; a wrong directional penalty can hurt more than spreading capacity evenly. Picture the flagship failure: on UCI HAR embeddings, always-matching the estimated direction is worse than abstaining on 6 / 6 6/6 cells—not because Matching is false, but because the estimate was not trustworthy.

sections.heading: The trust ratio.
sections.text: Write ε \varepsilon for a high-probability operator-norm bound on ‖ Σ ^ − Σ ‖ op \|\widehat{\Sigma}-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}} and γ = λ r − λ r + 1 \gamma=\lambda_{r}-\lambda_{r+1} for the eigengap of the top deployment subspace. The scalar that organises the decision is τ := ε γ = estimation uncertainty spectral separation . \tau\;:=\;\frac{\varepsilon}{\gamma}\;=\;\frac{\text{estimation uncertainty}}{\text{spectral separation}}. Small τ \tau : the estimated direction is identifiable; matching it is close to oracle Matching. Large τ \tau : do not trust the direction—even-spread remains the default. Davis–Kahan enters later as a proof tool that converts τ \tau into a subspace-error bound; it is not the idea.

sections.heading: What the math says vs. what we do.
sections.text: Under the LQ Matching response, for probes in the chosen top- r r deployment subspace the oracle-relative absolute drift gap scales as | D ^ − D ⋆ | ≲ C ⋅ τ 2 |\widehat{D}-D^{\star}|\lesssim C\cdot\tau^{2} (Theorem 3 )— O ⁡ ( τ 2 ) O(\tau^{2}) in the Davis–Kahan separation region τ < 1 / 2 \tau<1/2 , with practical usefulness depending on constants. Confidence-Calibrated Matching (CCM) is a policy that uses τ \tau : directional match, soft blend, or even-spread abstention. Its thresholds are frozen by a calibration protocol (§ 7 )—not a corollary of the theorem—but the match threshold sits inside that separation region; most of the soft band does not. Synthetic grids and identifiable positives (Fashion rotations) show the complementary regime where trust is warranted. Scope. Oracle-relative regret of estimated projector Matching under the LQ response (§ 2 )—not a new covariance estimator, not a new Davis–Kahan theorem, and not global optimality among regularisers. CCM thresholds are policy, not theorem. Deep / real blocks are experiments under a specified protocol, not a nonlinear Matching extension. Optional companions ( Rajput (2026b) , Rajput (2026a) ) motivate why geometry matters and what coverage means; this paper restates the LQ objects it needs and is readable alone.

sections.heading: 3 Related work
sections.text: We situate by distinction: same tools, different question.

sections.heading: Coverage design.
sections.text: Rajput (2026b) and Rajput (2026a) supply the cover question and even-spread default. Distinction: we ask when an estimate of that geometry is trustworthy enough to match.

sections.heading: Classical matrix tools.
sections.text: Operator-norm covariance bounds ( Vershynin, 2018 ) , spiked models ( Johnstone, 2001 ) , Davis–Kahan / Wedin ( Davis and Kahan, 1970 ; Yu, Wang, and Samworth, 2015 ) , and Ledoit–Wolf shrinkage ( Ledoit and Wolf, 2004 ) are ingredients or baselines. Distinction: we package ε / γ \varepsilon/\gamma as τ \tau and prove that Matching drift gaps scale as τ 2 \tau^{2} on the chosen top- r r subspace under the LQ response—not a new matrix inequality.

sections.heading: Domain shift and DRO.
sections.text: CORAL ( Sun and Saenko, 2016 ) , DANN ( Ganin et al., 2016 ) , DRO / group-robust training ( Ben-Tal et al., 2009 ; Rahimian and Mehrotra, 2019 ; Sagawa et al., 2020 ) , and IRM / DG benchmarks ( Arjovsky et al., 2019 ; Gulrajani and Lopez-Paz, 2021 ) address shift with different objectives and usually without a Matching coverage certificate. Distinction: CCM is a finite-sample gate on Matching, not a competitor to those programmes.

sections.heading: Closest concurrent.
sections.text: Landers (2026) regularise along an estimated drift subspace and report tolerance to moderate subspace misspecification. Distinction: their object is pathwise volatility under a frozen predictor; ours is oracle-relative Matching drift regret as a function of τ = ε / γ \tau=\varepsilon/\gamma , with CCM as a calibrated match/soft/abstain map.

sections.heading: Selective prediction.
sections.text: Selective classification ( Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017 ; El-Yaniv and Wiener, 2010 ) abstains on uncertain labels . Distinction: CCM abstains from directional geometry matching , falling back to even-spread rather than refusing a prediction.

sections.heading: 5 The trust ratio
sections.text: Estimation error alone does not decide whether matching is trustworthy. A large eigengap can absorb moderate covariance error; a tiny gap makes small ε \varepsilon fatal. The decision object is the ratio of those two scales. Definition 1 (Trust ratio) . Let ε ⁡ ( n , δ ) \varepsilon(n,\delta) be a high-probability bound on ‖ Σ ^ − Σ ‖ op \|\widehat{\Sigma}-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}} and γ := λ r − λ r + 1 > 0 \gamma:=\lambda_{r}-\lambda_{r+1}>0 the eigengap cutting the top- r r deployment subspace. The trust ratio is τ := ε ⁡ ( n , δ ) γ . \tau\;:=\;\frac{\varepsilon(n,\delta)}{\gamma}. (2) Numerator: how uncertain the estimate is. Denominator: how identifiable the subspace is. Operational reading—before any perturbation lemma: τ ≪ 1 \tau\ll 1 means the direction is identifiable enough to match; τ ≫ 1 \tau\gg 1 means spread the penalty; τ = O ⁡ ( 1 ) \tau=O(1) is the soft band in between.

sections.heading: 6 What the theorem says
sections.text: Proofs: Appendix A . The intellectual object is τ = ε / γ \tau=\varepsilon/\gamma . Large estimation error relative to the eigengap means: do not trust the subspace. Davis–Kahan converts that ratio into a projector gap; the LQ Matching response then converts the projector gap into an oracle-relative drift gap. Neither conversion is the idea— τ \tau is.

sections.heading: What this does—and does not—say.
sections.text: As τ → 0 \tau\to 0 , estimated projector matching recovers oracle matched drift at rate τ 2 \tau^{2} for probes in range ⁡ ( Π W ) \mathrm{range}(\Pi_{W}) . Large τ \tau does not justify trusting W ^ \widehat{W} ; even-spread ( Σ ′ ∝ I \Sigma^{\prime}\propto I ) remains the no-axis default ( Rajput, 2026a ) . The bound is oracle-relative regret under correct second-moment specification—not absolute optimality among regularisers, and not a numerical recipe for CCM thresholds. Those thresholds are a calibrated policy (§ 7 ). The theorem gives O ⁡ ( τ 2 ) O(\tau^{2}) scaling in the Davis–Kahan separation region τ < 1 / 2 \tau<1/2 ; practical usefulness depends on constants (Remark 11 ). CCM’s match threshold sits inside that separation region; most of the soft band does not. We state the theorem for projectors to isolate subspace error through τ \tau . Full Σ ^ \widehat{\Sigma} matching adds bulk eigenvalues that can shrink task directions (Appendix 12 ); experiments therefore treat full Σ ^ \widehat{\Sigma} as the dangerous naive baseline and the projector as CCM’s match arm.

sections.heading: 7 How CCM uses it
sections.text: Theorem 3 motivates a decision rule: trust Π W ^ \Pi_{\widehat{W}} when τ \tau is small; distrust it when τ \tau is large. Confidence-Calibrated Matching (CCM) turns that motivation into one penalty with three arms—match, soft blend, even-spread abstention.

sections.heading: Policy, not corollary.
sections.text: CCM is an operational map from τ \tau to a penalty. Its thresholds are fixed by the calibration protocol below and then frozen. They are not implied by Theorem 3 . The soft band is a calibrated heuristic; most of it sits outside the proved Davis–Kahan separation region τ < 1 / 2 \tau<1/2 , where Theorem 3 gives O ⁡ ( τ 2 ) O(\tau^{2}) scaling (constants decide numeric usefulness).

sections.heading: 8 Experiments
sections.text: The flagship claim is failure avoidance: when τ \tau says do not trust the direction, blindly matching hurts. Supporting blocks check that τ \tau tracks subspace error, that CCM wins when the direction is identifiable, and that a practical ε \varepsilon opens those regimes on real features. Theorem 3 is linear–quadratic and oracle-relative; the blocks below are experiments under a specified protocol—not a proof that CCM is optimal for every architecture. Code: experiments/ ; frozen numbers: results/index.json and results/exp0*/summary.json .

We quantify that decision by the trust ratio τ = ε / γ \tau=\varepsilon/\gamma (estimation uncertainty over spectral separation). Under the linear–quadratic Matching response, oracle-relative drift between estimated and oracle projector matching scales as τ 2 \tau^{2} for probes in the chosen top- r r deployment subspace— O ⁡ ( τ 2 ) O(\tau^{2}) in the Davis–Kahan separation region τ < 1 / 2 \tau<1/2 , with practical usefulness depending on constants. Experiments show both regimes, including UCI HAR embeddings where always-match is worse than abstain on every cell. † † heading: 0 2026 1-1 8/26 † † shortheadings: When Can We Trust the Matching Principle? / Rajput † † firstpage: 1 keywords matching principle, trust ratio, deployment geometry, Davis–Kahan, confidence-calibrated matching 1 Introduction Suppose Matching would be optimal if the deployment direction were known. We estimate it, regularise aggressively—and do worse than isotropic. The problem is not whether directional matching is sharp; it is whether the direction is identifiable. Match only geometry you can identify; otherwise spread the penalty. That is the whole decision. Finite samples scramble subspaces when the eigengap is small; a wrong directional penalty can hurt more than spreading capacity evenly. Picture the flagship failure: on UCI HAR embeddings, always-matching the estimated direction is worse than abstaining on 6 / 6 6/6 cells—not because Matching is false, but because the estimate was not trustworthy. The trust ratio. Write ε \varepsilon for a high-probability operator-norm bound on ‖ Σ ^ − Σ ‖ op \|\widehat{\Sigma}-\Sigma\|_{\mathrm{op}} and γ = λ r − λ r + 1 \gamma=\lambda_{r}-\lambda_{r+1} for the eigengap of the top deployment subspace. The scalar that organises the decision is τ := ε γ = estimation uncertainty spectral separation . \tau\;:=\;\frac{\varepsilon}{\gamma}\;=\;\frac{\text{estimation uncertainty}}{\text{spectral separation}}. Small τ \tau : the estimated direction is identifiable; matching it is close to oracle Matching. Large τ \tau : do not trust the direction—even-spread remains the default. Davis–Kahan enters later as a proof tool that converts τ \tau into a subspace-error bound; it is not the idea. What the math says vs. what we do. Under the LQ Matching response, for probes in the chosen top- r r deployment subspace the oracle-relative absolute drift gap scales as | D ^ − D ⋆ | ≲ C ⋅ τ 2 |\widehat{D}-D^{\star}|\lesssim C\cdot\tau^{2} (Theorem 3 )— O ⁡ ( τ 2 ) O(\tau^{2}) in the Davis–Kahan separation region τ < 1 / 2 \tau<1/2 , with practical usefulness depending on constants. Confidence-Calibrated Matching (CCM) is a policy that uses τ \tau : directional match, soft blend, or even-spread abstention. Its thresholds are frozen by a calibration protocol (§ 7 )—not a corollary of the theorem—but the match threshold sits inside that separation region; most of the soft band does not. Synthetic grids and identifiable positives (Fashion rotations) show the complementary regime where trust is warranted. Scope. Oracle-relative regret of estimated projector Matching under the LQ response (§ 2 )—not a new covariance estimator, not a new Davis–Kahan theorem, and not global optimality among regularisers. CCM thresholds are policy, not theorem. Deep / real blocks are experiments under a specified protocol, not a nonlinear Matching extension. Optional companions ( Rajput (2026b) , Rajput (2026a) ) motivate why geometry matters and what coverage means; this paper restates the LQ objects it needs and is readable alone. 2 LQ objects (self-contained preliminaries) A cold reader needs only the objects below. Notation follows Rajput (2026a) ; every formula used later is stated here. Displacements and second moments. Let Δ \Delta be a label-preserving input displacement with Σ = 𝔼 ⁡ [ Δ ​ Δ ⊤ ] ⪰ 0 \Sigma=\mathbb{E}[\Delta\Delta^{\top}]\succeq 0 . Large eigenvalues of Σ \Sigma are directions where deployment moves a lot. Linear–quadratic response. For a training penalty Σ ′ ⪰ 0 \Sigma^{\prime}\succeq 0 , probe v v , and weight λ > 0 \lambda>0 , w λ ​ ( Σ ′ , v ) = ( I + 2 ​ λ ​ Σ ′ ) − 1 ​ v , D Σ ​ ( w ) = w ⊤ ​ Σ ​ w . w_{\lambda}(\Sigma^{\prime};v)=(I+2\lambda\Sigma^{\prime})^{-1}v,\qquad D_{\Sigma}(w)=w^{\top}\Sigma w. Even-spread takes Σ ′ ∝ I \Sigma^{\prime}\propto I : no axis estimate; in this LQ response it strictly improves on task-only training when axes are unknown. Matched training takes Σ ′ \Sigma^{\prime} aligned with Σ \Sigma (or its top subspace): sharper when axes are known. Wrong-axis penalties leave a permanent floor. Operational rule used below: prefer even-spread unless the estimated geometry is trustworthy enough to match (§ 7 ). What this paper adds. The geometry to match is treated as given in the cover question above. We study Σ ′ \Sigma^{\prime} as a function of a finite-sample estimate Σ ^ \widehat{\Sigma} and ask when that choice stays close to oracle matched drift D Σ ​ ( w λ ​ ( Π W , v ) ) D_{\Sigma}\bigl(w_{\lambda}(\Pi_{W};v)\bigr) . The answer is organised by τ = ε / γ \tau=\varepsilon/\gamma (§ 5 – 6 ), not by a new cover theorem. 3 Related work We situate by distinction: same tools, different question. Coverage design. Rajput (2026b) and Rajput (2026a) supply the cover question and even-spread default. Distinction: we ask when an estimate of that geometry is trustworthy enough to match. Classical matrix tools. Operator-norm covariance bounds ( Vershynin, 2018 ) , spiked models ( Johnstone, 2001 ) , Davis–Kahan / Wedin ( Davis and Kahan, 1970 ; Yu, Wang, and Samworth, 2015 ) , and Ledoit–Wolf shrinkage ( Ledoit and Wolf, 2004 ) are ingredients or baselines. CORAL ( Sun and Saenko, 2016 ) , DANN ( Ganin et al., 2016 ) , DRO / group-robust training ( Ben-Tal et al., 2009 ; Rahimian and Mehrotra, 2019 ; Sagawa et al., 2020 ) , and IRM / DG benchmarks ( Arjovsky et al., 2019 ; Gulrajani and Lopez-Paz, 2021 ) address shift with different objectives and usually without a Matching coverage certificate.
